lessons.learn: The same praise can carry irony and the same adjective can carry a refusal: さすがですね and ちょっと むずかしいですね depend entirely on what surrounds them. A C2 reader hears the pause before deciding what was said.

grammar.title: Irony and refusal
grammar.pattern: さすがですね · ちょっと むずかしいですね · そうですね、かんがえて みます
grammar.explain: Irony is carried by the pause and the context, not by the words: the same さすがですね praises or punctures. A refusal stays inside politeness — ちょっと, むずかしい, かんがえて みます — so that nobody has to be contradicted out loud.

lessons.title: リズム: 体言止めと とうご
lessons.learn: Rhythm in Japanese is punctuation and word order before it is vocabulary: 体言止め ends on a noun and lets the sentence hang, とうご pulls the emphasised word to the front. The line is read aloud to check the breath.

grammar.pattern: しずかな あさ。 · おどろいた、ほんとうに。 · リズムは よみての いきに あわせます

lessons.learn: At the limit of mediation the word is kept and the loss is written down. 木漏れ日 and 甘える are not translated away; they are glossed, and the gloss says ものたりない — what falls short.

grammar.title: Mediating the untranslatable
grammar.pattern: ことばを そのまま のこす · かっこに やくを つける · ものたりなさを かく
grammar.explain: The word stays in Japanese, the gloss goes in brackets, and the note records what the gloss left out. Refusing to translate is a decision with reasons, and the reasons are written down — ちんもく そのものが いみを もつ, and the reader is told so.

examples.r: Kakko ni yaku o tsukemasu.
examples.en: I attach a gloss in brackets.

culture.text: Japanese has a vocabulary for exactly the things translation loses: 木漏れ日 (light through leaves), 甘える (to lean on someone's kindness), おもてなし (the whole of hospitality), わびさび. A C2 writer treats them as untranslatable on purpose — keeps the word, glosses the sense, and records the gap, the way a museum labels an object it will not move. The same discipline governs rhythm: 体言止め (ending on a noun) and inversion carry the emphasis that English puts in stress.

reading.text: おもてなし、という ことばは せつめい しにくい。きゃくを まつ じかん そのものが おもてなし だからだ。えいごでは hospitality と やくされるが、その ことばが ふくむ ちんもく と まつ ことは うつらない。やくす のではなく、ことばを そのまま のこして、かっこで せつめいする ほうが しんじつに ちかい。
reading.gloss: The word omotenashi is hard to explain. That is because the very time of waiting for a guest is omotenashi. It is translated as 'hospitality', but the silence and the waiting that the word contains do not carry over. Rather than translating, leaving the word as it is and explaining it in brackets is closer to the truth.

listening.script:
調停者: その ことば、えいごで いえますか。
査読者: いえ、ちかづけますが、おなじには なりません。
調停者: じゃ、ことばを のこして、やくを つけますか。
査読者: はい。かっこの なかの やくは、ものたりなさ も かきます。
listening.gloss: Mediator: Can you say that word in English? Reviewer: No, one can get close, but it does not become the same. Mediator: Then shall we keep the word and attach a gloss? Reviewer: Yes. In the gloss in brackets I also write what falls short.

idioms.meaning: to fall short, to leave something missing
if we put it another way
to carry over, to be transferred

mistakes.wrong: その ことばは やくせますが、おなじ いみに なります。
mistakes.right: その ことばは やくせますが、おなじ いみには なりません。
mistakes.why: Untranslatability is a negative claim: …には なりません.

mistakes.wrong: ことば を のこす ほうが しんじつに ちかい です。
mistakes.right: ことばを のこす ほうが しんじつに ちかい。
mistakes.why: ほうが … ちかい ends in the plain form; no です.

mistakes.wrong: やく を つけますか, かっこ の なか に やく。
mistakes.right: ことばを のこして、かっこに やくを つけます。
mistakes.why: Japanese does not stack comma-separated fragments; the te-form links the two actions.

task.title: Gloss five untranslatable words and record the gap
task.instructions: Choose five Japanese words with no single English equivalent — 木漏れ日, 甘える, おもてなし and two of your own. For each, write three lines: the word in Japanese, a twenty-word English gloss that gets as close as it can, and a note beginning ものたりない: that names what the gloss dropped. Then write one sentence of your own using two of the five, in a register where they belong (a letter, a review, a spoken aside), and read it aloud for rhythm rather than meaning.
